terms.winRate:
Win Rate is the percentage of your closed trades that ended in profit. A break-even trade counts in the denominator and is not a win — the line under the number shows how many there were.

Win rate alone does not decide profitability: a trader at 40% can be profitable when the average win is larger than the average loss. Look at Profit Factor and Avg R too.
terms.profitFactor:
Profit Factor = total gross profit ÷ total gross loss, across closed trades.

Above 1 your trading made money net; below 1 it lost. With no losing trade there is nothing to divide by, so it shows ∞. It is computed before commissions — the app has no commission model.
terms.avgR:
Average R-Multiple per closed trade.

R = trade profit ÷ risk per share at the saved stop. The profit follows the direction of the trade: on a LONG it is (Exit − Entry), on a SHORT it is (Entry − Exit) — so a winning SHORT is always a positive R. +1.0R means you made exactly what you risked.

Only trades that had a stop can be measured in R — a trade without one is excluded from this average, not counted as 0R. The line under the number shows how many of your closed trades the average actually covers.
terms.expectancy:
Expectancy = (Win% × average winning R) − (Loss% × average losing R), with break-even trades in the denominator.

It shows how many R you expect to make per trade on average. Positive means you have an edge; negative means you lose over time regardless of individual wins. It is measured in R, not dollars, so it does not depend on position size.
terms.sharpe:
Per-trade Sharpe = mean R ÷ standard deviation of R, over closed trades.

It is a variant of the Sharpe ratio (Sharpe, 1994), which divides excess return by its variability. Here there is no risk-free rate and no annualizing — the unit is a trade, not a year — so the number is not comparable to a fund's or an index's Sharpe ratio. Higher means R outcomes that are steadier relative to their mean.
terms.maxDD:
Maximum Drawdown — the largest drop, in money, from a peak in your cumulative closed-trade P&L to the low that followed it.

It is in your display currency, not a percentage of capital. Smaller means better capital preservation. Deep drawdowns are hard to recover from: after a 25% drop you need about a 33% gain to get back to the peak.
terms.avgHold:
Average holding period per closed trade, in rounded calendar days. A trade opened and closed on the same day counts as 0.

Compare it with the Hold Time vs P&L chart in Analytics: it shows whether your longer or shorter holds are the ones that make money.
terms.equityCurve:
Your Equity Curve shows account balance over time: the capital base you set plus cumulative P&L, one point per closed trade, by closing day.

A curve that rises gradually means gains accumulating without sharp drops. Sharp jumps in either direction usually point to changing position size. Open positions are not included.
terms.totalReturn:
Your total profit or loss from closed trades, as a percentage of the capital base you set. Open positions are not included.

It is the headline performance number — but without risk context (max drawdown, average R) it does not tell the whole story.
terms.winStreak:
The number of profitable trades in a row, up to your latest closed trade. When the latest trade lost, the card shows 0 — a losing streak is not shown here as a negative number; it appears in Streak History in Analytics.

A winning streak builds confidence, but it is also a common time for overconfidence and unplanned increases in risk.
terms.grade:
A weighted grade for the month: 40% win rate, 30% R, 20% discipline and 10% consistency, on a 0–100 scale. A from 85, B from 70, C from 55, D from 40, and F below.

The discipline part relies on the 'followed my plan' flag on your trades — a self-report. It is a quick snapshot, not a substitute for digging into the details.
terms.entryQuality:
A (star) rating of how well your entry matched the planned setup: timing, price and confirmation. The rating is yours — the app does not measure it from prices.

A consistently high rating signals discipline — even when the trade itself loses.
terms.streakHistory: A record of your winning and losing streaks over time, from the same chronological pass that computes the current streak. It reveals patterns: does a losing streak make you trade worse (Tilt), or do you return to discipline.
terms.dayOfWeek: Your profit/loss broken down by day of the week, by entry day (not exit day). It shows which days you consistently make or lose money — check how many trades sit on each day before drawing a conclusion.
terms.performanceBySetup: A breakdown of every setup you trade — win rate, total R and number of trades, sorted by trade count. Shows at a glance which setups carry your account and which drain it.
terms.rr: Risk/Reward: potential profit versus what you risk, written risk:reward. 1:3 = you stand to make 3× your planned loss.
terms.rMultiple:
R-Multiple = trade profit ÷ risk at the saved stop. The profit follows the direction of the trade: on a LONG it is (Exit − Entry), on a SHORT it is (Entry − Exit) — so a winning SHORT is always a positive R.

+2R = you made 2× what you risked · −1R = you lost your planned risk · −2R = twice the planned loss (a stop not honored, or an opening gap past it).

Risk is measured against the stop saved on the trade: if you edited the stop after entry, R uses the new value. Tracking R removes dollar-size bias and lets you compare trades.
terms.mfeMae:
Maximum Favorable Excursion (MFE) — how far a trade ran in your favor before it closed. Maximum Adverse Excursion (MAE) — how far it ran against you.

Comparing them across trades helps tune stops and targets (Sweeney, 1997). You fill in the fields — with no value there is no measurement.
terms.wilson:
The Wilson score (Wilson, 1927) is the lower bound of a 95% confidence interval for a success rate. With few trades it sits well below the raw percentage, and it approaches it as the sample grows.

That keeps a short run of wins from ranking above a pattern proven over dozens of trades. The app uses it to rank Edge and Anti-Edge.
terms.rrBucket3plus:
The group of trades whose planned ratio — distance to target versus distance to stop — is 1:3 or more. It is the planned ratio, not the realized outcome.

The arithmetic: at 1:3 the break-even win rate is 1 ÷ (1 + 3) = 25%, before commissions. Above that the group is profitable — if the targets were actually reached.
terms.dna:
Your Trading DNA is four 0–100 scores computed from your closed trades:

Risk management — your average risk per trade as a percentage of capital. Discipline — the share of trades you marked 'followed my plan'. Consistency — the spread of your R outcomes. Growth — the slope of cumulative R over your last 20 trades.

Three are measured from the trades; discipline is a self-report. A score with no data shows as —, never as 50.
terms.edge:
Your Edge — up to 5 setup × emotion pairs where your results are strongest, from your trade history.

A pair qualifies only with at least 3 trades, and it is ranked by the Wilson score of its win rate times (1 + average R). It is a relative ranking, not a statistical significance test — on a small sample an edge can disappear.
terms.antiEdge:
Anti-Edge — up to 5 setup × emotion pairs where your win rate is below 50% or your average R is negative, for pairs with at least 2 trades.

Either fix them (study why they fail for you) or stop trading them. Avoiding anti-edges is as important as exploiting edges.
terms.tilt:
Tilt — an emotional state that makes you deviate from your trading rules. Common after large losses, missing a big move, or a winning streak that breeds overconfidence.

Signs: larger positions, more frequent trades, ignored stops. Tilt Shield warns on 3+ losses in a row, a trade soon after a loss, 4+ trades in a day, trading outside your hours, and 2 plan deviations in a week.

Rule of thumb: take a short break after a losing streak; Tilt Shield warns from 3.
terms.marketRegime:
Market Regime — the current market environment, read from real price action (not your trades). Computed from SPY/QQQ versus their 20-day average, trend %, how many sector ETFs are rising (breadth) and realized volatility.

• Bull Trend: price above a rising 20-day average with broad participation. Favor breakouts and pullbacks.
• Bear Trend: price below a falling 20-day average, broad weakness. Favor shorts or stand aside.
• Choppy/Range: no net trend — price stuck between support and resistance. Fade the extremes, avoid breakouts.
• High Volatility: large daily swings dominate. Rule of thumb: cut size ~50% and widen stops.
• Low Volatility: quiet, coiled tape — expect small moves.

Shows 'insufficient data' when there isn't enough price history to classify.
terms.discipline:
The share of your closed trades you marked 'followed my plan' — stop, size and target, without emotional deviation. An unmarked trade is not in the denominator.

It is a self-report: the app does not check whether the stop was actually honored.
terms.dnaRisk:
The risk score comes from your average risk per trade — distance to stop × shares, as a percentage of capital at entry. Up to 1% scores 100; each percentage point above that removes 50; 3% or more scores 0.

It does not measure whether you honored the stop or kept position size uniform — only how much you risked on average.
terms.dnaConsistency:
The consistency score comes from the standard deviation of R across closed trades with a stop: 1 − (standard deviation ÷ 3), and 0 from 3R up.

High means outcomes that resemble each other; low means results that hinge on a few extreme trades. It needs at least 2 trades with an R, otherwise it shows —.
terms.dnaGrowth:
The growth score comes from the slope of cumulative R over your last 20 closed trades with a stop. A flat slope = 50; +1R per trade or more = 100; −1R or less = 0.

It measures a trend in results, not learning: a rising score means cumulative R is climbing over your recent trades.
terms.riskPerTrade:
Maximum risk per trade as a percentage of your capital base — what you lose if the stop is hit. Position size and the cap on all open positions are derived from it.

Rule of thumb: up to 2% per trade (Elder). Many professional traders risk closer to 1%.
terms.riskLimits:
Two limits work together:

• Risk/Trade — the most you risk on a single position. You choose this in Settings.
• Max Allowed Risk — the most you risk across ALL open positions combined. It is derived from Risk/Trade: twice that value, never below 3% and never above 5%.

Divide Max Allowed Risk by Risk/Trade to see how many full-size positions you can hold at once.
terms.positionSize:
Position Size = (Account Size × Risk %) ÷ (Entry − Stop Loss)

Example: $10,000 account, 1% risk, $100 entry, $97 stop:
Position = $100 ÷ $3 = 33 shares

Always calculate before entry. Never size by feel.
terms.stopLoss:
Stop Loss — the price level where you exit a losing trade to prevent larger losses.

Place it at a logical technical level:
• Below key support (LONG trades)
• Above key resistance (SHORT trades)
• Never arbitrary (e.g., 'just $0.50 below entry')

R and position size are computed from the stop saved on the trade.
terms.takeProfit:
Take Profit — your target price for exiting a winning trade.

The app's default — in the chart actions and the coach — is a 1:2 ratio: a target twice as far as the stop.

Common practice:
• Scale out: part at 1R, the rest to target
• Use technical levels (resistance, prior highs)
• Never lower the target while the trade is winning
terms.breakout: Price breaking above a key resistance level with volume. Best in trending markets.
terms.pullback: Buying when an uptrending price temporarily retraces toward support — a moving average, a prior breakout level, or a trendline — then resumes higher. Entering on the dip gives a better price and a tighter stop than chasing.
terms.bullFlag: Tight consolidation after sharp move up. Volume should contract during the flag.
terms.ORBBreakout: Opening Range Breakout — a break of the first 5, 15 or 30 minutes' high/low. Strong on trend days.
terms.VWAPReclaim: Price reclaiming VWAP after a morning dip, on volume.
terms.higherLow: Each pullback makes a higher low than the previous. Cleanest setup in uptrend.
terms.cupAndHandle: U-shaped consolidation with tight handle on right. Classic continuation pattern.
terms.failedBreakout: Breakout that quickly reverses. Trap for late buyers — SHORT when price falls back below the breakout level.
terms.overextendedFade: Counter-trend trade when price is unusually far above the 20 EMA, often with a high RSI. Requires patience.
terms.EMABounce50: Pullback to 50 EMA on daily chart. Major support in strong uptrends.
terms.trendContinuation: Entry on shallow pullback to 9 EMA in established trend. Tight stops, high R.
terms.gapAndGo: Stock gaps up at open and continues higher without filling. Best with news catalyst.
terms.earningsGapPlay: Trade the gap reaction after earnings, in either direction: a gap up — LONG above the opening high; a gap down — SHORT below the opening low. Hold winners and exit at the first sign of a move against you.
terms.rangeBreakout: Price breaking out of multi-day/week range. Most reliable when volume expands.
terms.postEarningsStrength: Stock holds above gap-up after earnings beat. Institutional accumulation signal.
terms.powerHourBreak: Breakout in last hour (3-4pm ET). Institutional positioning into close.
terms.MOCFade: Market-On-Close fade. Trade against extended moves into close for next-day reversal.
terms.overnightHold: Trade held overnight. Higher reward potential but exposed to gap risk.
terms.overnightReversal: Trade reversal of overnight move at market open. Counter-trend, requires confirmation.
terms.supportBounce: Buying when price drops to a known support level and reverses up. The logic: buyers defend the level. The stop sits below support — if it breaks, the thesis is void.
terms.resistanceBreak: Entering when price breaks above a resistance level that previously capped it, ideally on high volume. The break signals buyers have taken control. Differs from a generic Breakout by targeting one specific level.
terms.pullback20EMA: Buying when an uptrending price pulls back to the 20-period moving average and bounces. The 20 EMA acts as dynamic support; this setup combines trend with a precise entry point.
terms.emotionConfident: Confidence grounded in analysis, not bravado. When based on a valid setup it drives disciplined execution; when it tips into overconfidence after a win streak, it becomes risky.
terms.emotionCalm: The optimal emotional state for a trader. Calm lets you follow your plan without chasing or panicking. Trades opened calmly tend to respect their stop and target.
terms.emotionPatient: Waiting for a setup that genuinely meets your criteria instead of entering every move. Patience is often what separates a profitable trader from a losing one — it filters out low-quality trades.
terms.emotionNeutral: Entering with no emotional charge — neither excited nor fearful. A stable state that allows objective, data-driven decisions. A solid baseline, even if less sharp than "Calm".
terms.emotionHesitant: Hesitation at entry — usually a sign the setup isn't clear or confidence is low. Hesitant entries tend to mean entering late, placing the stop too tight, or exiting early out of fear.
terms.emotionNervous: Tension that clouds decision-making. Nervousness leads to obsessive price-checking, moving the stop, and impulsive exits. Often a sign the position is too large or the setup isn't trusted.
terms.emotionFOMO: "Fear Of Missing Out" — entering a trade just because price moved sharply, with no valid setup. One of the most destructive patterns: late entry, chasing price, and a distant stop. A red flag.
terms.emotionAngry: Anger after a loss — the fuel of "revenge trading". In this state a trader tries to win back a loss immediately, raises risk, and takes bad trades. This is how accounts blow up. Stop.
terms.chartCalcPosition: Auto-fills the Position Calculator from the current chart — ticker, live price as entry, a protective stop and a 1:2 target — then opens it so you can size the trade in one click.
terms.chartAddToJournal: Starts a new journal trade from the current chart — ticker, live price, a suggested stop and a 1:2 target pre-filled — ready for you to review and save.
